div.div: Understand the structure, quality, and operational value of your data by exploring CIM alignment, onboarding signals, datamodel coverage, acceleration suitability, and field composition.

div.p: What this shows: A quality indicator derived from observed structure, consistency and CIM alignment characteristics.
Why it matters: Data that is easier to interpret, classify and align is generally easier to operationalise, govern and investigate.
Read it as: This is an indicator, not a certification. Use it as a starting point for investigation and review the supporting evidence in DIG IN: Data Quality before drawing conclusions.

search.query: | eval structure_score=round(structure_ratio*100,0) | eval consistency_score=round(max(0,min(100,100-(shape_ratio*100)-(length_variance*25))),0) | stats avg(structure_score) as Structure avg(consistency_score) as Consistency | eval Structure=round(Structure,0), Consistency=round(Consistency,0) | appendcols [ $base_search$ | head $sample_limit$ | fieldsummary maxvals=1 disable_derived_fields=true | rename field as field_name | eval field_name=lower(trim(field_name)) | where NOT match(field_name,"^_") | stats dc(field_name) as current_fields | join type=inner max=0 field_name [ | inputlookup datamodel_fields_lookup | eval field_name=lower(trim(field_name)) | fields field_name ] | stats dc(field_name) as matched_dm_fields | eval "CIM Alignment"=round(if(current_fields>0,(matched_dm_fields/current_fields)*100,0),0) | fields "CIM Alignment" ] | eval Overall=round((Structure+Consistency+'CIM Alignment')/3,0) | table Overall Structure Consistency "CIM Alignment" | transpose 0 column_name="Quality Dimension" | rename "row 1" as "Score"

div.p: What this shows: The observed distribution of structured, semi-structured, unstructured and inconsistent telemetry within the selected analysis scope.
Why it matters: Data structure influences parsing consistency, field extraction opportunities and downstream analysis capabilities.
Read it as: Classification is based on observed characteristics within sampled events. It provides evidence of structure patterns, not a judgement of business value or usefulness.

search.query: | stats count as count by Classification | sort Classification

div.p: What this shows: The underlying structure characteristics used to assess the selected source population, including structure ratio, shape diversity and event length variance.
Why it matters: Different data sources often exhibit different formatting patterns, which can affect consistency, parsing reliability and analysis outcomes.
Read it as: Higher structure ratios generally indicate more consistently formatted telemetry. They do not automatically indicate higher quality or greater operational value.

search.query: | fields group_value structure_ratio shape_ratio length_variance | rename group_value as "Data Source" | sort "Data Source"

div.p: What this shows: Average, percentile and maximum delivery lag by the selected grouping, calculated by comparing Splunk index time (_indextime) with the timestamp parsed onto the event (_time).
Why it matters: Delivery lag can affect whether telemetry is available when searches, dashboards, detections or operational reviews expect it to be available.
Read it as: This is comparative delivery evidence, not a root-cause finding. Future timestamp evidence is intentionally excluded here and handled separately in Timestamp Integrity by $group_by$.

search.query: | where delay_category!="Future timestamp" | stats count as "Events Checked" avg(ingest_delay_seconds) as avg_lag_seconds median(ingest_delay_seconds) as median_lag_seconds perc95(ingest_delay_seconds) as p95_lag_seconds max(ingest_delay_seconds) as max_lag_seconds values(timeliness_rule_source) as "Rule Source" by group_value | eval "Average Lag"=case( abs(avg_lag_seconds) < 60, tostring(round(avg_lag_seconds,0)) . "s", abs(avg_lag_seconds) < 3600, tostring(round(avg_lag_seconds/60,1)) . "m", abs(avg_lag_seconds) < 86400, tostring(round(avg_lag_seconds/3600,1)) . "h", true(), tostring(round(avg_lag_seconds/86400,1)) . "d" ) | eval "Median Lag"=case( abs(median_lag_seconds) < 60, tostring(round(median_lag_seconds,0)) . "s", abs(median_lag_seconds) < 3600, tostring(round(median_lag_seconds/60,1)) . "m", abs(median_lag_seconds) < 86400, tostring(round(median_lag_seconds/3600,1)) . "h", true(), tostring(round(median_lag_seconds/86400,1)) . "d" ) | eval "P95 Lag"=case( abs(p95_lag_seconds) < 60, tostring(round(p95_lag_seconds,0)) . "s", abs(p95_lag_seconds) < 3600, tostring(round(p95_lag_seconds/60,1)) . "m", abs(p95_lag_seconds) < 86400, tostring(round(p95_lag_seconds/3600,1)) . "h", true(), tostring(round(p95_lag_seconds/86400,1)) . "d" ) | eval "Max Lag"=case( abs(max_lag_seconds) < 60, tostring(round(max_lag_seconds,0)) . "s", abs(max_lag_seconds) < 3600, tostring(round(max_lag_seconds/60,1)) . "m", abs(max_lag_seconds) < 86400, tostring(round(max_lag_seconds/3600,1)) . "h", true(), tostring(round(max_lag_seconds/86400,1)) . "d" ) | rename group_value as "Data Source" | table "Data Source" "Events Checked" "Average Lag" "Median Lag" "P95 Lag" "Max Lag" | sort - "Events Checked" "Data Source"

div.p: What this shows: Timestamp integrity indicators by the selected grouping, including events where the parsed event timestamp (_time) is ahead of the Splunk index time (_indextime).

Why it matters: Future timestamps are important to spot quickly because they commonly indicate source clock skew, timezone handling or timestamp parsing issues. Future-dated events can be missed by time-bounded searches and detections until the event time becomes current.

Read it as: This identifies timestamp evidence that warrants review. Use DIG IN: Telemetry Delivery to identify the affected source population and inspect representative events before deciding on corrective action.

search.query: | stats count by group_value timestamp_indicator | where count>0 | chart sum(count) over timestamp_indicator | rename group_value as "Data Source" | sort "Data Source"

div.p: What this shows: Current datamodel alignment and potential alignment opportunities for Splunk CIM datamodels.

Why it matters: Current alignment shows datamodel field coverage where the expected top-level CIM tag is observed. Potential alignment shows field coverage for datamodels where matching fields exist but the top-level tag is not observed.
Read it as: Use Field scope to compare required/recommended fields or all datamodel fields. Use the Data Readiness IN drilldown for the field and tag evidence behind each result.

search.query: | inputlookup datamodel_fields_lookup | stats count by datamodel | sort datamodel

| where in_datamodel=1 | where "$field_scope$"="all" OR model_field=1 | eval datamodels=if(isnull(datamodels),"__none__",datamodels) | mvexpand datamodels | rename datamodels as datamodel | eval selected_dm=if(len("$datamodel_filter$")=0,"*","$datamodel_filter$") | eval selected_dm_wrapped="|" . selected_dm . "|" | eval datamodel_norm=replace(datamodel," ","_") | where selected_dm="*" OR like(selected_dm_wrapped,"%|*|%") OR like(selected_dm_wrapped,"%|" . datamodel . "|%") OR like(selected_dm_wrapped,"%|" . datamodel_norm . "|%") | stats dc(field_name) as matched_scope_fields values(observed_tags) as observed_tags by datamodel | join type=left max=0 datamodel [ | inputlookup datamodel_fields_lookup | eval datamodel=trim(datamodel) | eval selected_dm=if(len("$datamodel_filter$")=0,"*","$datamodel_filter$") | eval selected_dm_wrapped="|" . selected_dm . "|" | where selected_dm="*" OR like(selected_dm_wrapped,"%|*|%") OR like(selected_dm_wrapped,"%|" . datamodel . "|%") | eval field_name=lower(trim(field_name)) | eval recommended=if(recommended="true" OR recommended=1,1,0) | eval required=if(required="true" OR required=1,1,0) | eval scope_field=case( "$field_scope$"="all",1, "$field_scope$"="recommended" AND (recommended=1 OR required=1),1, true(),0 ) | where scope_field=1 | stats dc(field_name) as total_scope_fields by datamodel ] | eval datamodel_key=case( lower(datamodel)="inventory","Compute_Inventory", lower(datamodel)="java virtual machines","JVM", true(),replace(datamodel," ","_") ) | eval observed_tags=mvmap(observed_tags, lower(trim(observed_tags))) | join type=left max=0 datamodel_key [ | inputlookup cim_datamodel_tags_lookup | eval datamodel_key=trim(datamodel) | eval expected_tag=lower(trim(expected_tag)) | eval tag_role=lower(trim(coalesce(tag_role,"supporting"))) | where tag_role="top_level" | fields datamodel_key expected_tag ] | eval top_level_tag_observed=if(isnotnull(expected_tag) AND mvfind(observed_tags, expected_tag)>=0,1,0) | stats max(top_level_tag_observed) as top_level_tag_observed max(matched_scope_fields) as matched_scope_fields max(total_scope_fields) as total_scope_fields by datamodel | eval field_alignment_pct=if(total_scope_fields>0,round((matched_scope_fields/total_scope_fields)*100,2),0) | eval current_alignment_pct=if(top_level_tag_observed=1,field_alignment_pct,0) | eval potential_alignment_pct=if(top_level_tag_observed=0,field_alignment_pct,0) | where current_alignment_pct>0 OR potential_alignment_pct>0 | eval "Current Alignment %"=case("$dm_perspective$"="operational" OR "$dm_perspective$"="current" OR "$dm_perspective$"="combined",current_alignment_pct,true(),null()) | eval "Potential Alignment %"=case("$dm_perspective$"="potential" OR "$dm_perspective$"="combined",potential_alignment_pct,true(),null()) | table datamodel "Current Alignment %" "Potential Alignment %" | sort - "Current Alignment %" - "Potential Alignment %" datamodel

div.p: What this shows: Data sources where observed fields align with one or more CIM datamodels, but the top-level CIM tag was not observed.

Why it matters: Datamodel field alignment can indicate that telemetry may contain data relevant to a CIM use case. Without the top-level datamodel tag, that alignment may not be discoverable through tag-driven searches, datamodel workflows or CIM-based content.

Read it as: This highlights potential gaps between field evidence and top-level CIM tagging evidence. Absence of observed tags is not proof that tags are missing, only that they were not detected within the selected scope and sample population.

html.div: These sources contain fields that match CIM datamodels, but the top-level datamodel tag was not observed. Review these as potential tagging or onboarding opportunities rather than automatic tag recommendations.

search.query:
| where in_datamodel=1 | mvexpand datamodels | rename datamodels as datamodel
| eval observed_tags=mvmap(observed_tags, lower(observed_tags))
| join type=inner max=0 datamodel [ | inputlookup cim_datamodel_tags_lookup | eval datamodel=trim(datamodel) | eval expected_tag=lower(trim(expected_tag)) | eval tag_role=coalesce(tag_role,"supporting") | where tag_role="top_level" | stats values(expected_tag) as expected_tags by datamodel ]
| mvexpand expected_tags | eval has_expected_tag=if(mvfind(observed_tags, expected_tags)>=0,1,0)
| stats max(has_expected_tag) as has_expected_tag max(events_checked) as events_checked dc(field_name) as matched_dm_fields values(field_name) as matching_fields values(expected_tags) as related_cim_tags values(observed_tags) as observed_tags by group_value datamodel
| where has_expected_tag=0
| eval gap_severity=case( matched_dm_fields>=20, "High", matched_dm_fields>=10, "Medium", true(), "Low" )
| rename group_value as "Data Source" | rename datamodel as "Potential Datamodel" | rename events_checked as "Events Checked" | rename matched_dm_fields as "Matched DM Fields" | rename related_cim_tags as "Top-Level CIM Tags" | rename observed_tags as "Observed Tags" | rename matching_fields as "Matching Fields" | rename gap_severity as "Gap Severity"
| table "Data Source" "Potential Datamodel" "Gap Severity" "Events Checked" "Matched DM Fields" "Top-Level CIM Tags" "Observed Tags" "Matching Fields" | sort "Gap Severity" - "Matched DM Fields" "Data Source"

div.p: What this shows: Controls for comparing observed fields against CIM-related field usage models.
Why it matters: Understanding field utilisation patterns can help highlight differences between available telemetry and detected CIM relevance.
Read it as: This is analysis evidence, not a recommendation to remove, suppress or discard data. Additional fields may still have operational, investigative, governance or business value.
What this shows: The composition of observed fields compared with the selected datamodel field model.
Why it matters: Field composition provides context for understanding telemetry complexity, diversity and CIM alignment characteristics.
Read it as: Fields that are not currently associated with CIM are not necessarily unnecessary. They may support operational, investigative, governance or business-specific requirements.

search.query: | eval field_category=if(keep_field=1,"Matched DM Fields","Non-matched Fields") | stats dc(field_name) as field_count by group_value field_category | xyseries group_value field_category field_count | fillnull value=0 "Matched DM Fields" "Non-matched Fields" | rename group_value as "Data Source"

div.p: What this shows: The proportion of observed fields that fall outside the selected datamodel field model.
Why it matters: Comparing sources using a consistent model can help identify differences in field composition and CIM alignment.
Read it as: Higher percentages indicate greater divergence from the selected model. They do not indicate that fields should be removed without further review.

search.query: | stats dc(field_name) as current_fields dc(eval(if(would_drop=1,field_name,null()))) as dropped_fields dc(eval(if(keep_field=1,field_name,null()))) as matched_fields by group_value | eval "Field Reduction %"=if(current_fields>0,round((dropped_fields/current_fields)*100,2),0) | eval "Field Reduction Status"=if(matched_fields=0,"No datamodel field alignment detected","Modelled") | rename group_value as "Data Source" | table "Data Source" "Field Reduction %" | sort - "Field Reduction %"

div.p: What this shows: Detailed field-level evidence supporting the field utilisation model for each selected source population.
Why it matters: Reviewing field-level evidence provides transparency into how utilisation indicators and reduction estimates were produced.
Read it as: This view exists to support investigation and understanding. It should not be interpreted as a directive to remove fields or change ingestion behaviour.

search.query: | stats dc(field_name) as current_fields dc(eval(if(would_drop=1,field_name,null()))) as dropped_fields dc(eval(if(keep_field=1,field_name,null()))) as future_fields dc(eval(if(in_datamodel=1,datamodels,null()))) as matched_datamodels by group_value | eval field_reduction_pct=if(current_fields>0,round((dropped_fields/current_fields)*100,2),0) | rename group_value as "Data Source" | rename current_fields as "Data Fields" | rename dropped_fields as "Non-matched Fields" | rename future_fields as "Matched DM Fields" | rename matched_datamodels as "Matched Datamodels" | rename field_reduction_pct as "Field Reduction %" | table "Data Source" "Data Fields" "Non-matched Fields" "Matched DM Fields" "Matched Datamodels" "Field Reduction %" | sort - "Field Reduction %"

div.p: What this shows: The acceleration status of datamodels that have observable alignment within the selected analysis scope.
Why it matters: Acceleration status can influence the performance characteristics of searches and analytics that rely on those datamodels.
Read it as: Acceleration status is operational context only. It does not indicate whether acceleration should be enabled, disabled or modified.

search.query: | join type=inner max=0 field_name [ | inputlookup datamodel_fields_lookup | eval field_name=lower(trim(field_name)) | eval datamodel_alias=case( lower(datamodel)="inventory", "compute_inventory", lower(datamodel)="java virtual machines", "jvm", true(), datamodel ) | eval datamodel_norm=replace(lower(datamodel_alias),"[^a-z0-9]","") | fields datamodel datamodel_norm field_name ] | stats dc(field_name) as "Matched DM Fields" by datamodel datamodel_norm | join type=left max=0 datamodel_norm [ | rest /services/data/models | rename title as rest_datamodel | eval datamodel_alias=case( lower(rest_datamodel)="compute_inventory", "compute_inventory", lower(rest_datamodel)="jvm", "jvm", true(), rest_datamodel ) | eval datamodel_norm=replace(lower(datamodel_alias),"[^a-z0-9]","") | eval acceleration_enabled=case( acceleration=1 OR acceleration="1" OR acceleration="true", "yes", isnotnull(acceleration), "no", true(), "unknown" ) | eval acceleration_summary_range=coalesce('acceleration.earliest_time',"") | fields datamodel_norm rest_datamodel acceleration_enabled acceleration_summary_range ] | eval "Acceleration Enabled"=coalesce(acceleration_enabled,"not found") | eval "Summary Range"=coalesce(acceleration_summary_range,"") | table datamodel "Matched DM Fields" "Acceleration Enabled" "Summary Range" | sort - "Matched DM Fields" datamodel

p.strong: DIG is designed to help Splunk administrators, data owners, governance stakeholders, Security and Observability engineers identify data readiness concerns and decide what to investigate next.

div.p: If the remediation path is unclear, start with your Splunk platform team or data owners. If you need support turning DIG findings into an onboarding plan, CIM alignment work, governance improvements, Enterprise Security readiness or Observability readiness activity, Dev/Null Security can help.
